1.title: Security
1.text: Welcome to Module 8: Security. This module is in the Container Orchestration domain, and it covers the topic called Security. By the end you will be able to do four things. Describe security through the lifecycle phases, and the older four Cs. Trace an A P I request through authentication, authorization and admission. Grant access with R B A C and Service Accounts, using least privilege. And apply Pod Security Standards, security Context and supply chain controls.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Locks the Doors
1.text: At Harbor Books, developers may look at Pods in the shop namespace, but only the delivery pipeline may change them. The orders Pods must run with as few privileges as possible. Only trusted, checked images may run, and the payment key must stay secret. In this module you decide who may do what, and what a Pod may do.

1.title: Security Through the Lifecycle
1.text: The current Kubernetes docs follow the C N C F lifecycle phases of cloud native security: Develop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime. In Develop you build a threat model, review code, and adopt zero trust, which means never trust, always verify. In Distribute you secure the supply chain. You scan images, use certificates or signatures, and keep a private registry. In Deploy you control what is deployed, who deploys it and where. And in Runtime you protect access, compute and storage. Exam tip: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime. Security follows the software through its life.

1.title: The 4 Cs of Cloud Native Security
1.text: This slide is tagged old wording. Older Kubernetes docs and study material describe the four Cs of cloud native security: Cloud, Clusters, Containers and Code. Security is layered, and each layer builds on the layer outside it. Strong outer layers help the inner ones, and weak outer layers cannot be repaired in code. The current docs use the lifecycle phases instead, so know both vocabularies. Exam tip: Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code, from the outside in.

1.title: The API Request Path
1.text: Every request to the A P I server meets T L S, and then three checks, in order. Authentication asks who you are. It uses client certificates, tokens, bootstrap tokens, and JSON Web Tokens for service accounts. Failure gives four hundred and one. Authorization asks what you may do. R B A C is the usual mode, and a denial gives four hundred and three. Admission may modify or reject objects being created, changed or deleted, but it never acts on reads. One more fact: Kubernetes has no User object, because users come from outside. Exam tip: who are you, what may you do, is the object acceptable.

1.title: RBAC: Roles and Bindings
1.text: R B A C has four kinds. A Role holds permissions in one namespace. A Cluster Role is not namespaced, and covers cluster-wide or cluster-scoped resources. A Role Binding gives a role to subjects, meaning users, groups or Service Accounts, in a namespace. A Cluster Role Binding gives it cluster-wide. A Role Binding can also point at a Cluster Role, to reuse it inside one namespace. Permissions are additive, and there are no deny rules. Follow least privilege: avoid wildcards, and keep cluster admin for when it is truly needed. Exam tip: a role says what, a binding says to whom, and nothing denies.

1.title: An RBAC Role
1.text: Here is a Role in the shop namespace. A rule names A P I groups, resources and verbs. The empty string is the core group, so the rule covers Pods and Pod logs. The verbs are get, list and watch, so it is read-only. Other common verbs are create, update and delete. Resource names narrows a rule to named objects. And a Role Binding then gives this Role to a user, group or Service Account. Exam tip: a Role lists what is allowed, and the binding says to whom.

1.title: ServiceAccounts
1.text: A Service Account is the identity for Pods and automation. A user is for people. A Service Account lives as an A P I object in a namespace. Users live outside Kubernetes, and there is no User object. A Service Account gets a short-lived, rotating token through the Token Request A P I, while users use certificates, tokens and other methods. Every namespace gets a default Service Account when it is created. A Pod runs as a Service Account, and you give that account permissions with R B A C. And automount Service Account Token set to false stops a Pod from mounting a token, for Pods that never call the A P I. Exam tip: Service Accounts are for Pods, and users are for people.

1.title: Admission Control and Policy Engines
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Admission controllers run after authentication and authorization, and before the object is stored. They may mutate, which sets defaults, or validate, which accepts or rejects. Only mutating ones change the object. With webhooks, mutating ones run first, then validating ones. Validating Admission Policy is a built-in, declarative option for validation, with rules written in the Common Expression Language, C E L. And policy engines such as Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper, O P A for short, and Kyverno enforce rules through admission. Gatekeeper uses C R Ds for constraint templates and constraints. Kyverno writes policy as code. Exam tip: admission sees changes to objects, never reads.

1.title: Pod Security Standards and Admission
1.text: Pod Security Standards define three levels. Privileged is unrestricted, and allows known privilege escalations. Baseline is minimally restrictive, and prevents known privilege escalations. Restricted is heavily restricted, and follows current hardening best practices. Pod Security admission is the built-in controller that applies a level to a namespace, using labels such as pod security enforce baseline. The mode decides the effect. Enforce rejects the Pod. Audit adds an audit annotation. Warn shows a warning. Pod Security Policy is gone, and Pod Security admission replaces it. Exam tip: the level says how strict, and the mode says what happens.

1.title: securityContext
1.text: A security Context sets privilege and access settings for a Pod, or for one container. A container's settings override the Pod's where they overlap. Common settings are to run as non-root, to block privilege escalation, to use a read-only root filesystem, to drop capabilities, and to set a sec comp profile. The snippet locks down the orders container. It runs as non-root with the runtime default sec comp profile, and the container drops all capabilities. Allow privilege escalation is true when you leave it unset, so set it to false. Exam tip: drop everything the container does not need.

2.title: Protecting Secrets and Traffic
2.text: Several controls protect data and traffic. For Secrets, enable encryption at rest, limit access with least-privilege R B A C, and consider an external secret store. Base sixty-four is not encryption. T L S protects traffic to the Kubernetes A P I. A Network Policy limits which Pods may talk to which, as in Module 6, and it needs a plugin that enforces it. A service mesh can encrypt and authenticate traffic between services with mutual T L S. And granting list on Secrets lets the holder read their contents. Exam tip: defense in depth. No single control is enough.

2.title: Image Supply Chain Security
2.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Trust the image from build to run. Scan images for known vulnerabilities, called C V Es. A scanner such as Trivy also lists the packages inside, which is an S B O M. Sign images and verify the signature before use. Cosign, from Sigstore, signs container images. Keep images in a private registry that lets only authorized clients pull. And at deploy time, an admission policy, for example in Kyverno, can verify signatures. Exam tip: scan, sign, store privately, verify at admission.

2.title: Runtime Security and Auditing
2.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Four runtime tools. Sec comp filters the system calls a process may make. App Armor restricts programs with profiles. Falco, a C N C F graduated tool, watches kernel events such as system calls against rules, and alerts on abnormal behavior. And the audit log is a chronological record of A P I actions, with levels None, Metadata, Request and Request Response. Exam tip: restrict with sec comp and App Armor, detect with Falco, and record with the audit log.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Security
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Authentication, authorization or admission: who you are, what you may do, whether the object is acceptable. Role or Cluster Role: one namespace, or cluster-wide, and a Role Binding can reuse a Cluster Role in one namespace. R B A C rules are additive, with no deny. Service Account or user: Pods and a namespaced object, or people and external. Pod Security level or mode: Privileged, Baseline, Restricted, then enforce, audit, warn. And lifecycle phases or four Cs: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime now, and Cloud, Clusters, Containers, Code in older material. Exam tip: find the layer first.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. Layers: the lifecycle phases Develop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime, and the older four Cs. The request path is authentication, authorization, then admission, and there is no User object. R B A C uses Role and Cluster Role with bindings, it is additive, and it follows least privilege. Service Accounts are identities for Pods, with short-lived tokens. Admission is mutating then validating. Pod Security has the levels Privileged, Baseline and Restricted, the modes enforce, audit and warn, and the security Context. And for supply chain and runtime: scan, sign and use a private registry, then sec comp, App Armor, Falco and the audit log. Now nine practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which four lifecycle phases of cloud native security do the current Kubernetes docs use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The current docs follow the C N C F lifecycle phases: Develop, Distribute, Deploy and Runtime. Cloud, Clusters, Containers and Code are the four Cs of older material.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. In which order does the A P I server check an incoming request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The request is authenticated first, so the cluster knows who is asking. Then it is authorized, so the cluster knows what that user may do. Finally it passes through admission control, which can modify or reject the object.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Harbor Books wants developers to read Pods only in the shop namespace. Which objects achieve this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A Role limits permissions to one namespace, and a Role Binding gives it to the developers. A cluster-wide role breaks least privilege, Service Accounts are for workloads, and a Network Policy does not control A P I permissions.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which statement about R B A C permissions is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. R B A C permissions only add up. The rules of all applicable roles are combined, and there are no deny rules. A Role Binding can reference a Cluster Role to reuse it in one namespace, and a Role is namespaced.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A Harbor Books Pod never calls the Kubernetes A P I. How can the team reduce the risk from its A P I credential? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Turning off the automatic mount means the Pod holds no A P I token that an attacker could steal. Granting cluster admin does the opposite, Kubernetes has no User object, and recreating the namespace does not change how tokens are mounted.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. What can a mutating admission webhook do that a validating admission webhook cannot? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Mutating admission may change the object, and validating admission may only accept or reject it. Authentication comes earlier, and admission does not act on reads.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which Pod Security admission mode rejects a Pod that violates the chosen level? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The enforce mode rejects violating Pods. Audit and warn allow them, and baseline is a level, not a mode.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. The Harbor Books orders Pods must not gain extra privileges, and must not write to their root filesystem. Which security Context settings do this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Setting allow Privilege Escalation to false stops a process from gaining more privileges, and setting read Only Root Filesystem to true makes the root filesystem read-only. The other options widen access, or have nothing to do with a container's privileges.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which tool watches kernel events such as system calls and alerts on abnormal behavior at runtime? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Falco watches kernel events against rules and raises alerts at runtime. Cosign signs images, Trivy scans them, and Kyverno enforces policies at admission.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, D: Develop, Distribute, Deploy, Runtime. Question two, B: authentication, authorization, admission. Question three, A: a Role and a Role Binding limit access to one namespace. Question four, C: R B A C permissions are additive, with no deny. Question five, A: turn off the token mount. Question six, D: mutating admission can change the object. Question seven, B: the enforce mode rejects the Pod. Question eight, C: no privilege escalation, and a read-only root filesystem. Question nine, B: Falco watches kernel events.
